title: Readers, writers, files and paths
summary: The Read, BufRead and Write traits and why code should accept them generically, Cursor and Vec<u8> as in-memory streams, File, OpenOptions and file modes, BufReader and BufWriter, std::fs convenience functions, Path and PathBuf, directories and metadata, and io::Error.

blocks.md:
Rust's I/O is built on three traits in `std::io`:

- **`Read`**: something you can pull bytes from: `read(&mut buf)`, `read_to_end`, `read_to_string`, `read_exact`.
- **`BufRead`**: a reader with an internal buffer, which adds `read_line`, `lines()` and `split()`.
- **`Write`**: something you can push bytes into: `write_all`, `flush`, and the `write!`/`writeln!` macros.

Files, standard input and output, TCP sockets, byte slices and vectors all implement them. *Programming Rust* stresses the consequence: a function that takes `impl Read` or `impl Write` works with **all** of them, and can be tested in memory without touching the disk.

blocks.explain: `&mut output` works because `&mut W` implements `Write` whenever `W` does, so the caller keeps the vector. `lines()` strips the newline and yields `io::Result<String>`, since reading can fail mid-way.

blocks.title: Files and OpenOptions
blocks.md:
`File::open(path)` opens for reading; `File::create(path)` creates or **truncates** for writing. For anything else, *Rust in Action* uses **`OpenOptions`**, a builder that sets the mode flag by flag: `read`, `write`, `append`, `create`, `create_new` (fail if it exists), `truncate`.

Every system call is slow compared with memory. Reading a file byte by byte, or writing many small pieces, makes one call each. **`BufReader`** and **`BufWriter`** keep an 8 KB buffer in between. A `BufWriter` writes its remainder when dropped, but errors at that point are lost, so call `flush()` yourself when it matters.

blocks.title: Paths
blocks.md: File names are not always valid UTF-8 (Linux allows almost any bytes, Windows uses UTF-16), so Rust has its own string types for them: **`Path`** (borrowed, like `str`) and **`PathBuf`** (owned, like `String`), built on `OsStr`/`OsString`. *Rust in Action* calls this interacting with the file system "in a type-safe manner": `join` uses the right separator for the platform, and `file_name`, `extension`, `parent` and `components` take a path apart without string surgery. Converting to `&str` returns an `Option`, because it can fail.

blocks.title: io::Error
blocks.md: Every I/O operation returns `io::Result<T>`, an alias for `Result<T, io::Error>`. An `io::Error` has a **`kind()`** you can match on: `NotFound`, `PermissionDenied`, `AlreadyExists`, `UnexpectedEof`, and so on. That lets you treat "the file does not exist yet" differently from "the disk is broken":

blocks.title: Word count over any reader
blocks.md: Write `wc<R: BufRead>(input: R) -> io::Result<(usize, usize, usize)>` returning lines, words and bytes, like the Unix `wc`. Count bytes from each line's length plus its newline: use `read_line` in a loop (it keeps the `\n` and returns 0 at the end) rather than `lines()`, which drops it.
hints: `read_line` appends, so `line.clear()` at the start of each round.
`wc` counts newline characters as lines, which is why a last line without `\n` is not counted.

blocks.title: Text tools over readers and writers
blocks.goal: Write I/O code once against Read, BufRead and Write so it runs on files and in memory, and handle io::Error kinds.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn grep<R: BufRead, W: Write>(input: R, pattern: &str, out: W) -> io::Result<usize>`: write every line containing `pattern` as `"<line number>:<line>\n"` (numbers start at 1); return the number of matches.
- `pub fn parse_config<R: BufRead>(input: R) -> io::Result<HashMap<String, String>>`: lines `key = value`; trim both sides; skip blank lines and lines starting with `#`; a line without `=` is an error of kind `InvalidData` whose message mentions the line number, e.g. `"line 3: expected key = value"`.
- `pub fn save_lines(path: &Path, lines: &[&str]) -> io::Result<()>`: write the lines, each followed by `\n`, through a `BufWriter`, creating parent directories as needed.
- `pub fn load_lines(path: &Path) -> io::Result<Vec<String>>`: read them back; a missing file gives an empty `Vec` (not an error).
- `pub fn largest_file(dir: &Path) -> io::Result<Option<(String, u64)>>`: the name and size of the largest regular file directly inside `dir` (ignore subdirectories); `None` if there are none.
blocks.solution_explain: `grep` and `parse_config` never mention files, so the tests feed them byte slices and capture output in a `Vec<u8>`. `lines().collect()` into `io::Result<Vec<String>>` stops at the first error, as in chapter 13. Matching on `e.kind()` separates the expected missing file from real failures.

points: Read, BufRead and Write unify files, standard streams, sockets and memory.
Write functions generic over the traits and test them with byte slices and Vec<u8>.
OpenOptions controls the file mode; BufReader and BufWriter cut system calls; flush explicitly.
Path and PathBuf handle file names portably; std::fs covers whole-file and directory operations.
io::Error::kind() lets you handle expected failures like NotFound.
